---
title: Decorating symbols
---

<Callout>We significantly simplified the way how you create syntax sugar for symbool compared to how it is done in Mathematica. You can still use low-level boxes such as `RowBox`, `GridBox` and etc, but we do not recommend it since it violates SOLID principles</Callout>

Symbol decorations or syntax sugar - is one of the main selling point of Wolfram Mathematica and WLJS Notebook. Basic maths helpers such as fractions, square roots, integrals significatly increases the readabillity of input and output expression:


Morever, any [Plot](./../Plotting-Functions/Plot) or [Image](./../Image/Image) is in fact just a fancy output form of corresponsing `Graphics`, and `Image` expressions and fully editable! That's why the difference between input and output Wolfram Language cells in WLJS it rather wague.

Every symbol has it's __[InputForm](./../Formatting/InputForm)__ - this is how the expression can be typed by a user or serialized to a file, for example:

```wolfram
ListPlot[{0,1,2}] // InputForm
```

```wolfram
Graphics[{{}, Annotation[{{Annotation[{Directive[PointSize[0.012833333333333334], ...]}]}}]]
```

Then every symbol has it's output form - how it is displayed in the cell, or within other expressions. In WLJS we generally have 2 output forms:

- [StandardForm](./../Formatting/StandardForm) - what you see in all input/output [Wolfram Language](./../Cell-types/Wolfram-Language) cells;
- [WLXForm](./../Formatting/WLXForm) - what you see if the expression in placed on a [slide](./../Cell-types/Slide), [Markdown](./../Cell-types/Markdown) or [WLX](./../Cell-types/WLX) cells

If the output form is not defined - `InputForm` will be used, i.e. that's why all user-defined symbols look at they are in the output cells.

On the output expressions are processed with [MakeBoxes](./../Formatting/MakeBoxes) - an internal symbol, which is applied on any output. To define a form of expression, use `TagSet` pattern:

```wolfram
MySymbol /: MakeBoxes[MySymbol, StandardForm] := "6"
MySymbol /: MakeBoxes[MySymbol, WLXForm]      := "9"
```

Depending where this `MySymbol` is placed it will look and work diferently:

```markdown
.slide

## Have a look at

<SpecialSymbol/>
```

or

```wolfram
MySymbol
```

```wolfram
6
```

The given example on `StandardForm` alters not only the appearance, but also the output content: `MySymbol` is gone. __This is rather discuaraged__ in Wolfram Language, when you cannot get the original expression from the output. To address this issue, we shall go in depth on how to alter the displayed expression, but not the undelying one.

## Interpretation 

### Temporal

You can replace a symbol with an icon by applying [Interpretation](./../Formatting/Interpretation). After the first evaluation, the representation is lost and the true expression is revealed:

```wolfram
Interpretation[
  Graphics[Rectangle[{-1,-1},{1,1}], ImageSize->{20,20}], 
  1
]
```

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(1)(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*)
```

We can prove it by:

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(1)(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*) + 1
```

```wolfram
2
```

<Accordions>

<Accordion title="Magic Joystick">

We can create such structre, which looks like a [joystick](./../GUI/InputJoystick), but acts like a [dynamic symbol](./../Guides/Dynamic):

```wolfram
createDynamic2DSymbol[] := Module[{symbol = {0,0}}, With[{
    eventObject = InputJoystick[],
    helper = InputJoystick`IntegrationHelper[][Function[xy, symbol = xy]]
},
    EventHandler[eventObject, helper];
    Interpretation[eventObject, Offload[symbol]]
]]
```

Now we create one symbol like this:

```wolfram
createDynamic2DSymbol[]
```

and then __cut and paste__ it to let's say text position in `Graphics`:

```wolfram
Plot[Sin[x], {x, -5Pi, 5Pi}, Epilog->{
  Text["Sin[x]", (* HERE *), {0,0}]
}]
```

</Accordion>

</Accordions>


### Permament
To permamently change how the given symbol is displayed we should use `MakeBoxes`. Remeber, to apply `MakeBoxes` on any expression you want to provide to the output so it will propage down the tree:

```wolfram
morse[s_String];

morse /: MakeBoxes[m: morse[s_], f: StandardForm] := With[{
    i = Interpretation[Row[{"[", Style[s, 12], "]"}], m]
},
  MakeBoxes[i, f]
]
```

Let' define a helper constructor for our morse code:

```wolfram
morseTable = {"a" -> ".- ", "b" -> "-... ", "c" -> "-.-. ", 
  "d" -> "-.. ", "e" -> ". ", "f" -> "..-. ", "g" -> "--. ", 
  "h" -> ".... ", "i" -> ".. ", "j" -> ".--- ", "k" -> "-.- ", 
  "l" -> ".-.. ", "m" -> "-- ", "n" -> "-. ", "o" -> "--- ", 
  "p" -> ".--. ", "q" -> "--.- ", "r" -> ".-. ", "s" -> "... ", 
  "t" -> "- ", "u" -> "..- ", "v" -> "...- ", "w" -> ".-- ", 
  "x" -> "-..- ", "y" -> "-.-- ", "z" -> "--.. ", " " -> "/ "};

morse[s_String] := morse[StringReplace[ToLowerCase[s], morseTable]] /; StringMatchQ[s, ___~~WordCharacter..~~___];

morse /: TextString[morse[s_]] := StringReplace[s, 
  Map[Function[r, Rule[r[[2]], r[[1]]]], SortBy[Normal[morseTable], -StringLength[Last[#]] &]]];
```

Let's try to create a morse code container:

```wolfram
morse["sos"]
```

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(morse["... --- ... "])(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*)
```

To check that this is still `morse` symbol, apply `InputForm`:

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(morse["... --- ... "])(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*) //InputForm
```

```wolfram
morse["... --- ... "]
```

Let's convert it back to the text:

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(morse["... --- ... "])(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*) // TextString
```

```wolfram
"sos"
```

Finally, make it audible:

```wolfram
silence = Table[0, {t,0,40Pi,0.1}];
dot = Table[Sin[5 t], {t,0,40Pi,0.1}];
dash = Join[dot, dot];

morse /: Play[morse[t_String]] := With[{
  m = morse[t]
},
  Join @@ (Switch[#, ".", Join[dot, silence], "-", Join[dash, silence], _, Join[silence, silence]] & /@ StringSplit[m[[1]], ""]) // ListPlay // EmitSound;
];
```

```wolfram
(*VB[*)(morse["... --- ... "])(*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*) // Play
```


## ViewBox

<Cards>

<Card
    href="./Frontend-functions/Overview"
    title="Frontend symbols"
  >
    An advanced guide how to define frontend symbols and make them do funky stuff for you
  </Card>

</Cards>

Another way is to use Javascript with a custom display function. This can be done using [ViewBox](./../Formatting/Low-level/ViewBox). Let's firstly define our display function as [frontend symbol](./../Advanced/Frontend-functions/Overview):

```js
core.smileyDecorator = async (args, env) => {
    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = 50;
    canvas.height = 50;
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    // Draw a smiley face
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(25, 25, 20, 0, Math.PI * 2, true); // Outer circle
    ctx.moveTo(35, 25);
    ctx.arc(25, 25, 8, 0, Math.PI, false);  // Mouth
    ctx.moveTo(22, 20);
    ctx.arc(20, 20, 2, 0, Math.PI * 2, true);  // Left eye
    ctx.moveTo(32, 20);
    ctx.arc(30, 20, 2, 0, Math.PI * 2, true);  // Right eye
    ctx.stroke();
    //append to viewbox container
    env.element.appendChild(canvas);
}
```

Now we define a `StandardForm` for our symbol with `ViewBox` container. `ViewBox` allows to pass any decorator frontend symbol used to display an expression, and place any other expression underneath it in its `InputForm`:

```wolfram
SmileySymbol /: MakeBoxes[s_SmileySymbol, StandardForm] := With[{},
  ViewBox[s, smileyDecorator[]]
]

SmileySymbol[]
```

```wolfram

```

If you reevaluate the output cell, you will get the same decorated symbol. You can ensure that this is still the same symbol, by taking its first argument:

```wolfram
SmileySymbol[42]
```

```wolfram
SmileySymbol[42] // First
```

```wolfram
42
```


In this sence this syntax-sugar is not temporal, but permament. However we can apply the same trick as before an use it to decorate other expressions temporary:

```wolfram
Interpretation[SmileySymbol[], 1]
```

```wolfram
 - 1
```

```wolfram
0
```

### Indicators
Here is another example. Let's create a gauge, that can react on values changes. Define a gauge meter:

```wolfram
gauge[level_Real];

gauge /: MakeBoxes[g_gauge, StandardForm] := With[{},
  ViewBox[g, g]
]
```

Here we use identical display and input expressions, the last one has to be defined as a [frontend symbol](./Frontend-functions/Overview) too:

```js
.js

function setNeedlePosition(needle, value) {
    value = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, value));
    const angle = value * 180 - 90;
    needle.style.transform = `rotate(${angle}deg)`;
}

core.gauge = async (args, env) => {
  const gauge = document.createElement('div');
  gauge.style.width = '100px';
  gauge.style.height = '50px';
  gauge.style.border = '1px solid #000';
  gauge.style.borderRadius = '50px 50px 0 0';
  gauge.style.position = 'relative';
  gauge.style.background = 'linear-gradient(to right, red 0%, yellow 50%, green 100%)';

  const needle = document.createElement('div');
  needle.style.width = '2px';
  needle.style.height = '40px';
  needle.style.background = '#000';
  needle.style.position = 'absolute';
  needle.style.bottom = '0';
  needle.style.left = '50%';
  needle.style.transformOrigin = 'bottom';

  const pos = await interpretate(args[0], env);
  setNeedlePosition(needle, pos);

  gauge.appendChild(needle);
  env.element.appendChild(gauge);
}
```

Let's test it:

```wolfram
gauge[0.3]
```

You can also place it with other wolfram expressions

```wolfram
gauge[0.3] // Framed
```

For the next step we need to [define prototypes](./Frontend-functions/Overview) for our symbol to update the needle positon and enable instancing:

```js
core.gauge.update = async (args, env) => {
  const val = await interpretate(args[0], env);
  setNeedlePosition(env.element.firstChild.firstChild, val);
}

core.gauge.destroy = () => {}

core.gauge.virtual = true;
```

Now let's provide a symbol to `gauge` and manipulate it with a slider:

```wolfram
meterLevel = 0.5;
gauge[meterLevel // Offload]

EventHandler[InputRange[0,1,0.1], (meterLevel = #)&]
```

```

```



## ArrangeSummaryBox
This is somewhat default display structure in Wolfram Language shared across many symbols like `ColorData`, `NumericArray`, `ByteArray` and many more, that keeps the original expression hidden, and instead shows some stats, or details about the content.

For example, we have a symbol with information inside its arguments:

```wolfram
specialSymbol[<|"Date" -> Now, "Color" -> Red, "State" -> True|>]
```

Let's decorate it:

```wolfram
specialSymbol /: MakeBoxes[obj : specialSymbol[asc_Association], StandardForm] := 
    Module[{above},
        above = { 
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"Date: ", asc["Date"]}]},
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"Color: ", asc["Color"]}]}, 
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"State: ", asc["State"]}]}
        };

        BoxForm`ArrangeSummaryBox[
           specialSymbol, (* Head *)
           obj,           (* Input expression *)
           None,          (* Icon *)
           above,         (* Summary content *)
           Null
        ]
    ];
```

The result looks like this:

```wolfram
specialSymbol[<|"Date" -> Now, "Color" -> Red, "State" -> True|>]
```

```wolfram
specialSymbol[(*VB[*) <|"Date" -> DateObject[{2026, 2, 2, 11, 28, 25.895413`8.165797824213316}, "Instant", "Gregorian", 1.], "Color" -> RGBColor[1, 0, 0], "State" -> True|> (*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*)]
```

<Callout>

This is still valid input expression, unless it was too large and it will be indicated by a label: "Data is on Kernel", meaning that you can evaluate it in the current session still, but the data is not in the notebook and will be lost if you restart evaluation kernel.

</Callout>

Now add an icon based on the "Color" field. Note, that icon can only be `Image`, `Image3D`, `Graphics`, `Graphics3D`, `None` or any [frontend symbol](./../Advanced/Frontend-functions/Overview):

```wolfram
specialSymbol /: MakeBoxes[obj : specialSymbol[asc_Association], StandardForm] := 
    Module[{above, icon},
        above = { 
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"Date: ", asc["Date"]}]},
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"Color: ", asc["Color"]}]}, 
          {BoxForm`SummaryItem[{"State: ", asc["State"]}]}
        };

        icon = Graphics[{
          Lighter[asc["Color"]], Disk[{0,0}, 1],
          asc["Color"], Disk[{0,0}, 0.8]
        }, 
          ImageSize -> {50, 50}, 
          ImagePadding -> None, 
          Controls -> False,
          PlotRange -> {{-1,1},{-1,1}}
        ];

        BoxForm`ArrangeSummaryBox[
           specialSymbol,
           obj,
           icon,
           above,
           Null
        ]
    ];
```

```wolfram
specialSymbol[(*VB[*) <|"Date" -> DateObject[{2026, 2, 2, 11, 31, 53.514057`8.481042851597264}, "Instant", "Gregorian", 1.], "Color" -> RGBColor[1, 0, 0], "State" -> True|> (*,*)(*"1:"*)(*]VB*)]
```
